title: Everybody Has a Story
sub: Grades 5–8 · ELA · Biography and the oral-history interview
objective: Students read poster 2’s biography of Violet Dina Want as a mentor text: a claim about a person, made believable by specific details. They tell showing from telling, back a claim with evidence, then turn to the exhibition’s *Talk About It* guide to write open interview questions for a woman in their own family or community, and begin to write her story.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Most lives are never written down. Asking good questions, listening, and choosing the details that make a person real is how an ordinary life becomes a story others can keep.

items.text: find the specific details a biographer uses to show what a person was like
items.question: find the details a biographer uses to show a person?

items.text: back a claim about a person with evidence from a text, and explain it
items.question: back a claim about a person with evidence, and explain it?

items.text: write open interview questions that begin with How, What or Why, with follow-ups
items.question: write open interview questions, with follow-ups?

items.text: write a short biographical paragraph whose details show, not tell
items.question: write a paragraph whose details show, not tell?

materials: Poster 2 on a screen, or page 3 of this plan
*Talk About It* (in the *Who Gets Remembered?* room), if you have a screen
questions: Which single detail on poster 2 tells you most about Violet? Why that one?
What would you want to ask Violet, if you could?
Who wrote this biography, and how might that shape what it says?
What is one thing a woman in your family knows how to do that you would like to learn before it is forgotten?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the posters
connection: **Online,** *Talk About It* in the *Who Gets Remembered?* room has the full interview guide: what to do before, while listening and after, and fourteen questions to start with. **In the exhibition,** poster 2 and the *Violet’s Life* room.

steps.title: A claim about a life
script: Show poster 2’s last line without the rest: *“Violet Want’s life is a testament to resilience, humor, and hard work.”* Ask: *“Would you believe this about a stranger? What would a writer have to show you?”* Take answers; they are the lesson’s checklist.

screen.text: Violet Want’s life is a testament to resilience, humor, and hard work.
screen.cite: Poster 2 · Biography of a Working Class Woman

steps.purpose: Meet the biography’s claim before its evidence, and ask what would make it believable.
students: Would you believe this about a stranger?
What would a writer have to show you?

steps.title: Everybody
script: Then: The Smithsonian’s guide to collecting oral history puts it simply: “everybody has a story to tell.” *“Today we read how one family told one woman’s story, and get ready to collect one of our own.”*

screen.cite: The Smithsonian’s guide to collecting oral history

steps.purpose: Set the lesson’s turn: from Violet’s story to the stories students can collect.

steps.title: Claim and evidence
script: **Claim and evidence.** Read poster 2 together (page 3), and ask students to underline one detail for each word of the claim: *resilience, humor, hard work*. Three that work: she left school at 14 to help support her family; she said she chose Harold *“because he made her laugh”*; she could *“take apart adult coats, resize them, and reassemble them perfectly for her children.”*

screen.caption: Poster 2’s claim, and three of its details

cells: She continued to garden, even when rheumatoid arthritis made it difficult.
She married Harold … saying she had chosen him because he made her laugh.
She could take apart adult coats, resize them, and reassemble them perfectly for her children.

steps.purpose: See how a biographer backs each word of a claim with a specific detail.
students: Find another detail on the poster for one of the traits.

steps.title: Telling or showing?
script: **Telling or showing?** Put two sentences side by side: *“Widowed in 1956, Violet remained strong and resilient.”* and *“She continued to garden, even when rheumatoid arthritis made it difficult.”* The first tells; the second lets us see. A good biography needs both, but the details do the proving.

cells: Widowed in 1956, Violet remained strong and resilient.
She continued to garden, even when rheumatoid arthritis made it difficult.

steps.purpose: Tell a statement from a detail that lets the reader see for themselves.
students: Which one makes you see her?
Why might a writer need both?

steps.title: Questions that open
script: **Questions that open.** The exhibition’s *Talk About It* guide, drawn from the Smithsonian and the Library of Congress, says questions that begin with *How*, *What* or *Why* get better answers than *“Did you…?”*; ask one thing at a time; don’t be afraid of quiet moments; ask a follow-up, such as *“Can you give me an example?”* Model one closed question and its open version.

screen.caption: Questions that begin with How, What or Why get better answers than “Did you…?”

cells: What was school like for you? What is one thing a teacher said that you still remember?
What jobs have you done, inside or outside the home? How did you learn to do them?
Do you know how to cook?
What is something you know how to make, mend, grow or cook? Who taught you?

steps.purpose: Learn the first rule of a good interview from the exhibition’s guide.
students: What answer would each question get?
Write a follow-up for one of the questions on the right.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three read the same biography for evidence and plan an interview with a woman in their family or community.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Match six details from the biography to the trait each shows, turn three yes-or-no questions into open ones, choose interview questions, and write one sentence that shows instead of tells.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Build a claim, evidence and reasoning table for the biography, sort telling from showing and rewrite a telling sentence, and plan an interview of five questions, each with a follow-up.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Ask why a biographer includes small, surprising details and whose voice the poster leaves out, answer one of the exhibition’s reflection questions, and draft a biographical paragraph that opens with a claim and proves it.

steps.purpose: Read for evidence, plan an interview and write, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read Violet’s biography for evidence, then plan an interview of your own.

steps.title: Your turn to tell
script: Pairs read aloud their best interview question or their best showing sentence. Close with the exhibition’s own question: *“If the roles were reversed and you became the tradition-bearer, what stories would you like to tell?”*

screen.question: If the roles were reversed and you became the tradition-bearer, what stories would you like to tell?

steps.purpose: Turn the lesson around: students are the keepers of stories too.
students: Read your best question, or your best showing sentence, to a partner.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back: *“Can you now…?”* Thumbs up, sideways or down; ask a Red Level writer to read a sentence for the last.

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.
